title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident shows AI being used as a tool for social engineering fraud. The scammers used AI-generated emails to impersonate well-known public figures, specifically podcast hosts and their representatives, and to produce personalized correspondence that referenced accurate details about each target's career. The personalization is the mechanism that made the impersonation credible, replacing the generic phrasing that usually signals a scam with content specific enough to suggest insider knowledge.

The failure here is not in a deployed AI product but in the offensive use of AI-generated text outside any institutional system. There was no deployment pipeline to audit and no operator to intervene. The only check that could have caught the fraud was the recipients themselves verifying invitations through official channels before responding, something the apparent specificity of the messages was designed to prevent. Once a target was on a video call or had followed instructions about account settings, the social engineering had already succeeded.

What is not established is who is running the operation, what specific AI tools they used, or whether any of the described financial or account losses have been confirmed through independent verification.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

Fraudsters are running a sophisticated scam targeting Hollywood figures by impersonating famous podcasters and their representatives. Broadway performer Seth Rudetsky received a fake invitation from Nikki Glaser's podcast offering $4,000 to $5,000, complete with personalized details about his career that appeared authentic. Similarly, comedian Bruce Vilanch believed Terry Gross from NPR's Fresh Air wanted him as a guest. The scammers used AI-generated emails with impressive specificity and knowledge of the targets' work, making the invitations seem legitimate and establishing credibility through detailed correspondence.

The scams took different forms. Vilanch was eventually asked to send money to help NPR with funding issues before the fake interview occurred, and when he joined a video call, a stranger claiming to be Mike conducted it instead of Gross. Rudetsky was guided through Facebook permission settings and lost control of his social media account. Both men were initially fooled by the personalized approach and the apparent effort the scammers invested. Rudetsky continues receiving fraudulent podcast invitations from other celebrities and now sometimes engages the scammers to test their tactics. The scammers show no signs of stopping their operations.
